questions.why: It only flips layers' training flag. Use torch.no_grad() as well to skip building the graph.

questions.q: Why can NumPy add an array of shape (3, 1) to one of shape (1, 4)?
options: Broadcasting stretches both to shape (3, 4)
It flattens both arrays first
NumPy pads the smaller array with zeros
It fails unless the shapes match
questions.why: Dimensions of size 1 are repeated to match the other array, without copying the data.

questions.q: In a BatchNorm network, an EMA of the weights scores far worse than the raw weights. Likely cause?
options: Averaging the weights of a non-linear network always lands in a high-loss region
A small EMA decay makes it copy only the last noisy iterate, losing the benefit
The EMA weights are noisier than the final iterate, since averaging adds variance
BN running statistics don't match the averaged weights and need recomputing
questions.why: BN buffers were collected under the raw weights, not the averaged ones. Re-estimating them (or EMA-ing the buffers too) fixes it, as with SWA.

questions.q: What makes int8 quantisation of LLM activations hard at scale?
options: Attention scores overflow the int8 range inside the softmax computation
Rounding error accumulates linearly with the number of tokens processed
A few hidden dimensions hold huge outliers that stretch the range
The weights are too heavy-tailed to quantise to int8 without loss
questions.why: A handful of channels have values far larger than the rest. A shared scale set by them leaves most channels with only a few levels, hence mixed-precision schemes (LLM.int8).

questions.q: Averaging n predictors with pairwise correlation ρ: what does the ensemble variance approach as n grows?
options: A single model's variance divided by the correlation ρ
ρ times a single model's variance, a floor set by correlation
Zero, as long as every individual model is unbiased
Zero, as long as the models use different architectures
questions.why: Var = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/n. The second term vanishes but the first does not, so decorrelating members (as random forests do) matters more than adding members.

questions.q: How can two ReLU networks computing the same function have very different Hessian eigenvalues (sharpness)?
options: Hessian eigenvalues are only defined up to a global sign, so sharpness is ambiguous
The Hessian depends on the random initialisation, even for an identical function
Rescale one layer by c and the next by 1/c: same function, different curvature
Different mini-batches give different Hessians for the very same function
questions.why: ReLU's positive homogeneity allows such rescalings with identical outputs but different curvature (Dinh et al.). So raw Hessian sharpness is not a reliable predictor of generalisation.

questions.q: A VAE with a powerful autoregressive decoder reports KL near 0 and ignores z. What happened?
options: The reconstruction term is weighted too heavily against the KL penalty
The encoder variance blew up, so sampling noise swamps the latent code
The latent dimension is too small for the latent code to carry any information about x
Posterior collapse: the decoder models data alone, so q(z|x) matches the prior
questions.why: If the decoder can model x without z, the cheapest way to cut the KL term is to make the posterior equal to the prior. The latent then carries no information.

questions.q: A causal decoder-only transformer with no positional encoding still learns token order. How?
options: Token embeddings gradually absorb their index in the sequence during training
The causal mask gives each position a different number of visible tokens
Residual connections accumulate order information from layer to layer
LayerNorm's learned per-dimension bias encodes each token's position
questions.why: Under a causal mask, position t attends over exactly t tokens, and attention averages reveal that count. So order is recoverable, unlike in a bidirectional encoder.

questions.q: What does maximal-update parametrisation (μP) let you do when you widen a transformer?
options: Keep the compute per training step constant while the width grows
Tune the learning rate on a narrow proxy and reuse it on the wide model
Remove the normalisation layers without losing stability at any width
Reuse the narrow model's trained weights as the wide model's initialisation
questions.why: μP scales init and per-layer learning rates with width so that optimal hyperparameters stay roughly stable. Small-model tuning then transfers to a much larger model.

questions.q: A classifier separates your training rows from your test rows with AUC 0.9. What does that tell you?
options: Part of the test set has leaked into the training set
The classifier is overfitting, having memorised which rows belong to the training set
The features carry too little information about the target
Train and test differ in distribution, so validation scores may mislead
questions.why: If a model can tell where a row came from, the two samples are distributed differently (covariate shift). Validation on a different-looking sample can misestimate test performance.

questions.q: Lowering Adam's β2 from 0.999 to 0.95 cuts loss spikes in large LLM runs. Why?
options: It permanently shrinks the effective learning rate of all parameters, damping spikes
It makes bias correction unnecessary after the first few thousand steps
A lower β2 smooths the gradient direction more strongly, so spikes are damped
The second moment tracks a jump in gradient scale faster, so steps aren't oversized
questions.why: With β2 near 1 the second moment lags, so a sudden gradient surge yields a huge step. A shorter memory tracks the surge and divides it out.

questions.q: Why do many LSTMs initialise the forget-gate bias to a positive value such as 1?
options: So the output gate starts closed and the cell state stays hidden at first
So the cell remembers by default early on and gradients flow across long spans
To keep the cell state from growing without bound during the early phase of training
So the gates all start in the near-linear range of the sigmoid, near zero
questions.why: A positive bias pushes the forget gate toward 1, giving an almost identity cell path. This helps long-range gradients early in training (Jozefowicz et al.).

questions.q: In trained LLMs, heads often put large attention weight on the first token. Why?
options: The beginning-of-sequence embedding is initialised with a larger norm than the others
Softmax weights must sum to 1, so a harmless 'sink' absorbs spare attention
The first token holds a compressed summary of the entire prompt so far
Position 0 always receives the strongest positional signal in the model
questions.why: A head that has nothing useful to read must still distribute weight 1. Dumping it on a content-free token leaves the head's output roughly unchanged (attention sinks).

questions.q: In a BatchNorm network weight decay barely constrains the function. What does it mainly do instead?
options: It drives many weights exactly to zero, pruning channels as training proceeds
It shrinks weight norms, raising the effective learning rate of scale-invariant layers
It shrinks activations, which makes the batch statistics more stable across steps
It shrinks weight norms, lowering the effective learning rate as gradients get smaller
questions.why: BN makes the output invariant to weight scale, so only the direction matters. Smaller norm means larger angular updates per step, i.e. a higher effective learning rate.

questions.q: Why does test error peak where model capacity just reaches the interpolation threshold?
options: The only interpolating fit is ill-conditioned and amplifies label noise
Implicit regularisation from SGD is strongest at exactly that capacity
Training error is highest there, so the model is underfitting the data
Bias peaks there because the model has the least flexibility
questions.why: At the threshold there is just enough freedom to fit the noise, with no slack to choose a smooth interpolant. Beyond it, minimum-norm solutions spread the noise out and error falls again.

questions.q: CNNs with stride-2 downsampling aren't shift-invariant even though convolutions are shift-equivariant. Why?
options: Strided subsampling aliases, so a small shift changes the features
Batch normalisation makes the features depend on absolute position
The pooling windows are too small to cover the whole image at once
Zero padding breaks the shift-equivariance of the convolution itself
questions.why: Striding skips samples and violates Nyquist for high frequencies, so tiny shifts can change the output a lot. Blurring before subsampling (BlurPool) restores most invariance.

questions.q: Loss drops sharply the moment you cut the learning rate late in training. Why?
options: A smaller learning rate effectively raises the batch size of each gradient
Adam's bias correction finally stops distorting the second-moment estimate
Noisy large steps keep bouncing across the valley; small steps let it settle
The optimiser escapes a poor local minimum once the steps are small enough
questions.why: SGD noise scales with the learning rate and sets a floor on the loss. Annealing reduces that noise, so the iterate drops toward the valley floor.

questions.q: For a deep linear network with squared loss and full-rank data, which statement about critical points holds?
options: It has many bad local minima, since the loss is non-convex in the weights
Local minima are global only for networks with at most two layers
The loss is convex in the weights, so there are no saddle points at all
Every local minimum is global; the other critical points are saddles
questions.why: The loss is non-convex in the layer weights (so saddles exist), yet no bad local minima occur (Kawaguchi 2016). It is a benign non-convex landscape.

questions.q: Unregularised logistic regression is trained by gradient descent on linearly separable data. What happens?
options: Weights grow without bound, their direction nearing the max-margin separator
The weights keep oscillating between different separating directions
The loss plateaus at a nonzero value once the sigmoid outputs saturate
The weights converge to the finite maximum-likelihood solution, as in ordinary training
questions.why: On separable data the likelihood keeps improving as weights scale up, so there is no finite MLE. Gradient descent drifts to infinity, slowly, along the max-margin direction.

questions.q: You fit a single Gaussian q to a bimodal p by minimising KL(q‖p). What does q do?
options: Locks onto one mode and puts almost no mass on the other
Spreads out to cover both modes, centred between them
Becomes very broad so as to cover all of p's mass
Matches the mean and variance of p exactly, as in moment matching
questions.why: KL(q‖p) heavily penalises q putting mass where p is small, so it is mode-seeking. The forward KL(p‖q) would instead match moments and cover both modes.

questions.q: Why do Pre-LN transformers train stably with little warmup while Post-LN ones need it?
options: Pre-LN normalises activations twice as often, which bounds the weights
Pre-LN has fewer parameters, so there is less that can destabilise training
The identity residual path keeps gradients balanced across depth at init
Pre-LN makes attention scaling unnecessary, so the logits never saturate
questions.why: In Pre-LN the identity path bypasses LayerNorm, so gradient magnitudes stay balanced across layers at init. Post-LN gradients near the output are large, which needs warmup.

questions.q: At step 0 a 10-class classifier's loss is about 8, far above ln 10. What is the likely cause?
options: The learning rate is too high, so the very first steps overshoot into a bad region
The last layer's initial outputs are too large, so it starts confidently wrong
The batch is too small, so the loss estimate is far noisier than ln 10
The training labels are randomly shuffled relative to the inputs
questions.why: A sane init gives near-uniform predictions and loss close to ln K. A much larger value means big logits, which the learning rate cannot affect before the first update.

questions.q: Accumulating gradients over 8 micro-batches doesn't match a true 8x batch in a BatchNorm net. Why?
options: Each micro-batch is normalised by its own statistics, not the full batch's
BN's running averages are only updated on the last micro-batch, skewing eval
The optimiser takes eight times as many updates per effective step
The accumulated gradients get averaged in lower precision across micro-batches
questions.why: Accumulation sums gradients, but BN's forward pass sees only a small group at a time. Statistics, and thus the function being differentiated, differ from a big batch.

questions.q: Why can a zero-padded fully convolutional net tell where in the image an object sits, despite weight sharing?
options: The biases differ at every pixel position in the feature map
Max-pooling remembers the argmax coordinates and passes them to later layers
Border padding creates position-dependent responses that spread inward
Convolution kernels are flipped, which breaks the spatial symmetry
questions.why: Zero padding makes responses near the edges differ from interior ones, and deeper layers see further from the border, so absolute position can be decoded (Islam et al.).

questions.q: You multiply your loss by 1000 and plain SGD now diverges. What does Adam do?
options: Behaves almost identically, since its update divides out the gradient's scale
It takes about 1000 times smaller steps, since its second moment is inflated by the scale
It trains faster, since 1000 times larger gradients build momentum more quickly
It diverges too, since each Adam step is proportional to the gradient size
questions.why: Adam divides the momentum by the root of the second moment, so a constant gradient scale cancels (up to epsilon). SGD's step scales linearly with the loss.

questions.q: With several highly correlated, equally useful features, what does lasso tend to do?
options: Keep one of them and zero the others, somewhat arbitrarily
Share the weight equally among them, as ridge regression would
Give the largest weight to whichever of them is noisiest
Zero all of them, since each one is redundant given the others
questions.why: The L1 penalty has no reason to prefer splitting weight among duplicates, so it keeps one. Adding an L2 term (elastic net) groups correlated features.

questions.q: A classifier trained on balanced data goes live where positives are 1%. How can you fix its probabilities?
options: Apply Platt scaling that was fitted on the original training set
Re-standardise the input features using deployment-set statistics
Average each probability with the 1% base rate of the deployment
Reweight its odds by the ratio of deployment to training priors
questions.why: Under label shift, posterior odds scale by the prior ratio, a Bayes-rule correction. Fitting calibration on training data cannot capture the new prevalence.

questions.q: Past the critical batch size, what does doubling the batch size buy you?
options: A lower final loss at the same number of steps, since gradients are cleaner
Roughly half the steps, as in the small-batch regime where scaling is linear
A flatter minimum, and so reliably better generalisation on the test set
Almost no reduction in the number of steps, so mostly wasted compute
questions.why: Below the critical batch size, bigger batches cut steps almost proportionally. Above it, gradient noise is already low, so extra samples barely help.

questions.q: Stacked 3×3 convs that all use dilation 2 leave holes in the receptive field. Why?
options: Dilated kernels have zero weights in the gaps, so those never train
Each output sees only a sparse grid of input pixels, skipping those between
Dilation shrinks the feature map by discarding every other pixel row
Dilated convolutions cannot use padding, so a ring of border pixels is lost
questions.why: With a constant dilation, positions with different parity are never connected (the gridding effect). Using rates like 1, 2, 5 fills the gaps.

questions.q: Model A beats model B within every subgroup but has lower overall accuracy. How is this possible?
options: The subgroup accuracies were computed on the training data instead
Class imbalance inflates the overall accuracy of the weaker model
Overall accuracy is not a weighted average of subgroup accuracies
They were evaluated on different subgroup mixes (Simpson's paradox)
questions.why: If both are tested on the same data, overall accuracy is the same weighted average of subgroup scores, so A would win. A reversal needs different subgroup proportions.

questions.q: With 30% noisy labels, why does early stopping often beat training to convergence?
options: A high learning rate late in training cannot tolerate label noise
The noisy labels cancel out over the first few epochs of training
Validation loss is always lowest at the end of the first epoch
Nets fit clean, consistent patterns first and memorise the noise later
questions.why: Clean examples share learnable structure, so they are fit early. Random flips can only be memorised, which takes longer and hurts generalisation (Arpit et al.).

questions.q: Two classifiers differ by 0.4% accuracy on the same 2000 test examples. Which comparison is more powerful?
options: A two-sample t-test that treats the two test sets as independent
Comparing their training-set cross-entropy, which has less noise
A paired test on per-example disagreements, as their errors are correlated
Checking whether the two separate 95% confidence intervals for accuracy overlap
questions.why: Both models see the same examples, so most errors are shared. A paired test (McNemar, paired bootstrap) uses only the disagreements, giving much tighter inference than non-paired tests.

questions.q: Why does normalising queries and keys (QK-norm) stabilise large transformer training?
options: It makes the attention scores independent of the sequence length
It keeps the value vectors from growing and gradually inflating the residual stream
It bounds the attention logits, preventing softmax saturation and entropy collapse
It shrinks the key dimension, so the attention matrix needs less memory
questions.why: Unbounded query-key dot products can grow until attention is nearly one-hot, which gives tiny or spiky gradients. Normalising caps the logits.

questions.q: Why can't tree ensembles extrapolate a linear trend beyond the training range?
options: Random feature subsets hide the global trend from most trees
Their split thresholds assume uniformly distributed feature values
Predictions are averages of training targets, so stay inside their range
Bootstrap sampling tends to drop the extreme points of the data
questions.why: A leaf outputs a constant formed from training targets. Beyond the data the prediction is the last leaf's value, so the ensemble goes flat rather than following the trend.

questions.q: Why is the step-50k checkpoint of a 100k-step cosine run worse than a run scheduled for 50k steps?
options: The optimiser state is only meaningful at the very end of the schedule
Its learning rate is still high, so it lacks the final annealing phase
Weight decay accumulates over the longer schedule and hurts mid-run models
Cosine schedules need to see the whole dataset at least twice to work well
questions.why: Much of the final loss gain comes from the low-learning-rate tail. A mid-schedule checkpoint hasn't had it, which is why warmup-stable-decay schedules branch off a decay.

questions.q: In DPO, what plays the role of the reward?
options: A frozen reward model's score, applied to the chosen and rejected responses
The policy's log-probability of the chosen response, taken on its own
The KL divergence between the chosen and the rejected response distributions
β times the log-ratio of policy to reference probabilities of a response
questions.why: DPO's derivation shows the optimal KL-regularised policy defines an implicit reward equal to β log(π/π_ref) (up to a prompt-only term). No separate reward model is trained.

questions.q: k-means is the limit of a Gaussian mixture fit by EM under which condition?
options: Full covariances per cluster with the mixing weights held equal
Equal spherical covariances with variance shrinking to zero (hard assignments)
Any covariances at all, once k matches the number of true clusters
Diagonal covariances that are learned separately for each of the clusters in turn
questions.why: As the shared spherical variance goes to zero, the E-step responsibilities become 0 or 1 and the M-step becomes the centroid update, which is k-means.

questions.q: With very few training examples, naive Bayes often beats logistic regression. Why?
options: Its feature-independence assumption is usually true in real datasets
It is a discriminative model with fewer free parameters to fit
It optimises the conditional likelihood directly, which needs less data
Higher bias but lower variance, so it reaches its asymptote sooner
questions.why: The generative model converges quickly to its (worse) asymptotic error, while the discriminative model needs more data to catch up (Ng and Jordan).

questions.q: What does grouped-query attention shrink compared with standard multi-head attention?
options: The number of query heads, which cuts attention FLOPs proportionally
The KV cache, since several query heads share one key/value head
The softmax cost, because each token attends to fewer positions
The embedding table, because tokens in a group share one embedding
questions.why: GQA keeps many query heads but uses fewer key/value heads, shrinking the per-token cache that dominates memory at long context. Query count is unchanged.

questions.q: With 30% flipped labels, why does cross-entropy fit the noise more than a bounded loss like MAE?
options: It requires one-hot targets, and noise makes those targets more extreme
Its gradient peaks on confidently wrong examples, including mislabelled ones
Its minimiser shifts under symmetric noise, so it targets the flipped labels
It weights every example equally, so flipped labels count as much as clean ones
questions.why: CE gradient on an example grows as the model gets it more wrong, so flipped labels dominate. Bounded losses like MAE cap that, trading noise-robustness for slower fitting.

questions.q: Gradient boosting with depth-1 stumps can only represent which kind of function?
options: A piecewise-constant function of only the single most useful feature
A sum of functions, each depending on a single feature (additive)
A linear function of the features, since each stump is one split
A function containing at most pairwise interactions between features
questions.why: Each stump splits on one feature, so the sum is additive across features but each term can be a non-linear step function. Depth-d trees allow d-way interactions.

questions.q: A ReLU MLP trained on x in [-1, 1] is evaluated at x = 100. How does its output behave?
options: It decays toward zero, since the hidden units switch off far from the data
It saturates at roughly the value it had at the edge of the training range
It continues along a straight line, extending its last linear piece
It oscillates, repeating the pattern it learned over the training range
questions.why: A ReLU network is piecewise linear, and far from the data the active pattern stops changing. So the output is linear in the input there, not saturating or periodic.

questions.q: Why can dropout placed just before a BatchNorm layer hurt test accuracy?
options: Dropout masks keep resetting BN's running mean, so it never stabilises
BN already regularises, so any extra noise on top of it destroys the signal entirely
Variance differs between train and test, so BN's stored statistics mismatch
Dropout zeros BN's scale parameters during training, killing the layer
questions.why: In training, dropout inflates the variance BN sees; at test it is off, so the running variance no longer matches. This variance shift moves activations and costs accuracy.

questions.q: Random projection preserves pairwise distances among n points up to ε. What does the needed dimension depend on?
options: Linearly on the original dimension, since every coordinate must be kept
On ε only, since the number of points cancels out in the bound
On n and ε only, growing like log n, not on the original dimension
On the data's intrinsic rank only, never on the point count
questions.why: The Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma needs k = O(log n / ε²) dimensions regardless of the ambient dimension.

questions.q: Why does gradient boosting need a small learning rate while a random forest needs no shrinkage?
options: Boosted trees are deeper than forest trees, so they overfit more readily
Out-of-bag samples already shrink the forest's predictions toward the mean
Forest trees get pruned after training, while boosted trees do not
Boosting fits residuals in sequence, so large steps chase noise
questions.why: Each boosting stage fits the leftover error, noise included, so large steps overfit quickly. Forest trees are independent and averaging reduces their variance.

questions.q: Why does beam search tend to give dull, repetitive text in open-ended generation?
options: A wide beam covers too little of the vocabulary to find varied words
The likeliest sequences under the model are themselves bland and loopy
Beam search is biased toward very short outputs and pads with filler
Beams share prefixes, which makes the model overfit to repeated text
questions.why: In open-ended tasks, the most probable continuation is not the most human-like. Likelihood-maximising search finds loops and generic phrases (Holtzman et al.).

questions.q: Many self-attention layers are stacked with no residuals or MLPs. What happens to token representations?
options: Their norms grow exponentially with depth until the numbers overflow
They converge toward the same vector, so the output approaches rank one
They become mutually orthogonal across tokens as the depth increases
They stay unchanged, because attention merely permutes the tokens
questions.why: Each attention layer takes convex combinations of value vectors, which pushes tokens together. Skip connections and MLPs counteract this rank collapse (Dong et al. 2021).

questions.q: Impurity-based feature importance in random forests tends to be biased toward what?
options: High-cardinality or continuous features, which offer more split points
Features with the largest numeric scale, since splits are scale-based
Binary features, which can be split cleanly into two pure halves
Highly correlated features, each of which receives the full credit
questions.why: More candidate thresholds means more chances to find a chance-good split on training data. Permutation importance on held-out data is less affected.

questions.q: Why must a diffusion model see occasional condition dropout in training to use classifier-free guidance?
options: It makes the model robust to noisy or incorrect captions at test time
It trains an implicit classifier on noisy images alongside the denoiser
One network learns both conditional and unconditional predictions
It lowers the variance of the noise-prediction training loss itself
questions.why: Guidance combines the conditional and unconditional score predictions, amplifying their difference. Dropping the condition at random trains the unconditional branch in the same weights.

questions.q: Why can mean imputation hurt a model even when only 5% of values are missing?
options: It shrinks the feature's variance and weakens its link to the target
It always introduces leakage from the target into the feature
It biases the model only if values are missing completely at random
It shifts the feature's mean well away from the observed mean
questions.why: Filling with a constant adds points exactly at the mean, reducing spread and attenuating relationships. The mean itself is preserved, so that is not the issue.

questions.q: Late in training, validation accuracy still rises but validation NLL gets worse. How?
options: Accuracy and NLL are measured on different batches of validation data
The learning rate is too low for the probabilities to keep improving
It is underfitting, so its predicted probabilities drift toward uniform
The model grows overconfident, so its remaining mistakes cost ever more
questions.why: Pushing logits larger sharpens correct predictions but makes each wrong one cost a lot. Accuracy depends only on the argmax, NLL on confidence (Guo et al.).

questions.q: Why can PCA before k-NN help on high-dimensional noisy data?
options: Dropping low-variance directions removes noise that corrupts distances
PCA standardises the scale of every feature before the search
PCA makes the classes linearly separable before the neighbour search
PCA rotates the features, which makes k-NN invariant to rotation
questions.why: Many noise dimensions add distance without signal. Keeping top components removes much of it. k-NN with Euclidean distance is already rotation-invariant.

questions.q: GPT-2 scales residual-branch output weights at init by 1/√(number of layers). Why?
options: It keeps attention logits small so the softmax does not saturate at depth
It compensates for LayerNorm dividing out the standard deviation of the stream
It keeps the gradient norm of the embedding table constant across depth
Each block adds variance to the residual stream, which would grow with depth
questions.why: Summing N branch outputs into the stream grows its variance roughly linearly in N. Scaling each branch by 1/√N keeps the stream's scale roughly constant with depth.

questions.q: If you set Adam's epsilon to a huge value, what does the optimiser turn into?
options: A damped Newton method, using a diagonal estimate of the Hessian
signSGD, taking fixed-size steps in every coordinate regardless of gradient
SGD with momentum, with its effective learning rate divided by epsilon
RMSProp without momentum, since the first-moment term effectively vanishes
questions.why: The update is lr * m / (sqrt(v) + eps). When eps dominates, the denominator is a constant and what remains is an EMA of gradients, i.e. momentum SGD.

questions.q: Why does a mixture-of-experts layer need an auxiliary load-balancing loss?
options: Without it the router favours a few experts, which then win even more tokens
It forces every expert to specialise on a different syntactic category of token
Without it top-k routing is not differentiable and cannot be trained
Without it Adam cannot cope with experts whose gradient norms differ
questions.why: Routing is self-reinforcing: popular experts improve and attract more tokens, leaving the others undertrained. The auxiliary loss pushes toward roughly uniform usage.

questions.q: Why do labs train small models on far more tokens than compute-optimal scaling suggests?
options: More tokens steadily reduce the tokeniser's error rate on rare words
Compute-optimal ignores inference cost; a smaller model is cheaper to serve
Scaling laws stop applying once the parameter count is small enough
Small models overfit their few parameters unless they are shown many more tokens
questions.why: Compute-optimal scaling minimises training compute for a given loss. If a model is served a lot, extra training that shrinks the model saves far more at inference.

questions.q: Why can speculative decoding speed up generation without changing the output distribution?
options: The big model is quantised, so every forward pass runs somewhat faster
The draft model replaces the big one on easy tokens, accepted without checking
Low-probability tokens are pruned from the vocabulary before sampling
The big model verifies drafted tokens in parallel, with rejection sampling
questions.why: Verifying k tokens costs about one forward pass of the large model. Accept/reject steps make the final samples exactly match the large model's distribution.

questions.q: Why prefer the reparameterisation gradient over REINFORCE when z can be written as μ + σε?
options: Both are unbiased, but reparameterisation usually has far lower variance
REINFORCE cannot be combined with neural network function approximators
Reparameterisation also works directly for discrete latent variables
REINFORCE is biased unless a baseline is subtracted from the reward
questions.why: The pathwise estimator uses the gradient of f through the sample. The score-function estimator sees only f's value, which makes it noisy. Baselines cut variance but are not needed for unbiasedness.

questions.q: A credit model trained only on past approved applicants may mislead on all applicants. Why?
options: Concept drift between the approval date and the date of scoring
Class imbalance, since approved applicants rarely end up defaulting
Selection bias: outcomes of rejected applicants were never observed
Approved applicants are too few in number to train a model well
questions.why: The training sample was chosen by the previous policy, so the model never sees outcomes for the people it would now score differently. This is selection bias (reject inference).

questions.q: Why is LoRA's B matrix initialised to zero while A is random?
options: Zero B makes the update low-rank, which a randomly initialised B could not guarantee
Zero matrices compress well, so the saved adapter file is smaller
The pretrained weights are low-rank already, so B should start empty
The model starts exactly as pretrained, yet B still gets a nonzero gradient
questions.why: With B = 0 the update BA is zero, so the first forward pass matches the base model. A is random so B's gradient is nonzero and it learns from step one.

questions.q: A model always outputs the base rate as its probability and has ECE near zero. What does this show?
options: The model is well calibrated, so it must also be a good classifier
ECE is undefined for models whose outputs never vary across inputs
The base rate must have been estimated on the test set itself
Calibration says nothing about usefulness: it cannot tell cases apart
questions.why: A constant prediction equal to the prevalence is perfectly calibrated in bins yet cannot separate classes. Report discrimination (AUC) or a proper scoring rule too.

questions.q: Why can't a one-layer attention-only transformer do in-context copying ('... A B ... A' gives B)?
options: Without an MLP layer, the model cannot store anything about earlier tokens
Matching A to the token after its earlier occurrence needs two composed heads
A single attention head cannot attend to a token far back in the sequence at all
One layer has no positional information, so it cannot locate the earlier A
questions.why: Induction needs a previous-token head that tags each token with its predecessor, plus a second head that attends where that tag matches the current token. That composition needs two layers.

questions.q: Gradient descent from zero init on underdetermined least squares (more features than samples) finds which solution?
options: The minimum L2-norm solution among all that fit the data exactly
The minimum L1-norm solution, which is what the lasso would return
An arbitrary exact fit, which depends on the order of the mini-batches
The sparsest solution among those that fit the data exactly (minimum L0)
questions.why: Updates stay in the row space of X, and the only interpolant in that space is the pseudo-inverse solution with the least L2 norm. This is a simple implicit bias.

questions.q: A small transformer memorises modular addition fast but generalises thousands of steps later. What speeds this up?
options: Training on a smaller fraction of all possible pairs so there is less to memorise
Removing weight decay so the memorising solution can be refined further
Stopping as soon as training accuracy reaches 100%, before overfitting sets in
Stronger weight decay, which slowly favours the compact generalising solution
questions.why: Weight decay slowly erodes the high-norm memorising solution in favour of a lower-norm circuit that generalises. Less data or no decay delays or prevents grokking.

questions.q: A teacher trained with label smoothing often distils worse than an unsmoothed one. Why?
options: Smoothing flattens all outputs equally, so a lower distillation temperature is needed
The student cannot reach smoothed targets exactly, so its distillation loss never converges
Smoothing pulls same-class examples together, erasing which wrong classes are similar
Smoothed teachers fit the training set less well, so their soft labels carry more noise
questions.why: Smoothing collapses each class into a tight cluster, so the logits no longer say that a cat is closer to a dog than to a truck. That similarity signal is what the student learns from.

questions.q: Why is generating one token at batch size 1 limited by memory bandwidth rather than FLOPs?
options: Every weight must be read from memory for very little arithmetic
The softmax over the vocabulary must run serially across all tokens
Attention over the full prompt dominates the cost at every single step
Sampling forces the logits to be copied back to the CPU each step
questions.why: Each step multiplies a single vector by every weight matrix, so arithmetic per byte read is tiny. Batching or speculating amortises the weight reads.

questions.q: At temperature 0, a hosted LLM gives different outputs for the same prompt. Most likely cause?
options: Floating-point sums vary with batching and kernel order, flipping near-ties
Dropout is left switched on at inference time in the serving stack
Greedy decoding still samples randomly among the two or three likeliest tokens
The server's tokeniser adds a little random whitespace to each request
questions.why: Floating-point addition is not associative, and server batch composition changes reduction order. Tiny logit differences can flip a near-tied argmax, and the text then diverges.

questions.q: A CNN fits randomly shuffled ImageNet labels to zero training error. What does this show?
options: Its training error on the real labels is not a reliable quantity
It must therefore be memorising the real labels as well, and generalise poorly
Capacity alone cannot explain why it generalises on real labels
Its weights cannot have learned any real image features on the true labels
questions.why: The same model class can memorise noise, so bounds based only on capacity are vacuous. Generalisation must come from the data's structure and optimisation's implicit bias (Zhang et al.).

questions.q: If you change the class prevalence of the test set (same classifier, same per-class data), which pair is unaffected?
options: Precision and recall of the positive class
Overall accuracy and F1 score of the positive class
True-positive rate and false-positive rate
Precision and false-positive rate of the classifier
questions.why: TPR and FPR condition on the true class, so they don't depend on class proportions. Precision, accuracy and F1 mix classes and move with prevalence.

questions.q: After training with RandomResizedCrop at 224, why does testing at about 288 often improve accuracy?
options: Training crops magnify objects, so test objects look smaller than expected
Random crops destroy the global image structure, which larger inputs help restore
Larger inputs contain more information than the training images did
Larger inputs give the final pooling layer more pixels to average
questions.why: Random resized crops zoom in on objects, so the apparent object size at train time exceeds that of a centre crop at test time. Raising test resolution compensates (FixRes).

questions.q: You pick the 20 of 10,000 noise features most correlated with y, then cross-validate. Accuracy?
options: About chance, because the features contain no real signal
Exactly chance, but only if the folds are stratified
Well above chance, since selection saw the validation labels
Below chance, because the chosen features overfit the training folds badly
questions.why: Selection used all labels, so every fold's validation rows already influenced which features were kept. Selection must be done inside each training fold.

questions.q: On a quadratic loss, gradient descent diverges once the learning rate exceeds what?
options: 2 divided by the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian
The ratio of the largest to the smallest Hessian eigenvalue
2 divided by the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian
1 divided by the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian
questions.why: Along the top eigen-direction the error is multiplied by (1 − ηλmax) each step, whose magnitude exceeds 1 when η > 2/λmax. At 1/λmax it still converges.

questions.q: ELECTRA beats BERT at equal compute. What is the main reason?
options: Its generator is trained adversarially to fool the discriminator, as in a GAN
It uses a much larger vocabulary than BERT does at the same compute
Its discriminator learns from every token, not just the masked ~15%
It trains with a causal objective, which is stronger than masking
questions.why: ELECTRA detects which tokens were replaced by a small generator, a binary decision at every position. BERT's loss comes only from the few masked tokens.

questions.q: In Gaussian-process regression with fixed hyperparameters, what does the predictive variance at a test point depend on?
options: The targets' values, entering through the posterior mean
The spread of the observed targets around their mean value
Only the training inputs and the test point, not the targets
The size of the training residuals in the neighbourhood of the test point
questions.why: With a Gaussian likelihood the posterior covariance is a function of the kernel and the input locations alone. Targets move the mean, not the uncertainty.

questions.q: Why train a GAN generator with −log D(G(z)) rather than minimising log(1 − D(G(z)))?
options: It turns the game cooperative, so that training provably converges
Early on D rejects fakes, so log(1−D) gives vanishing generator gradients
It guarantees the optimum of the original minimax game is reached
It aligns the loss with the Wasserstein distance between the data
questions.why: When D(G(z)) ≈ 0 the saturating loss is flat in the generator's parameters. The non-saturating form has strong gradients exactly when the generator is losing.

questions.q: FlashAttention does the same FLOPs as standard attention but is much faster. Why?
options: It skips attention between tokens that are far apart in the sequence
It computes the attention scores in lower precision, which is faster
It approximates the softmax with a low-rank kernel to avoid the N×N matrix
It tiles the work so the N×N score matrix never goes to slow GPU memory
questions.why: Attention is bound by memory traffic, not arithmetic. Fusing and tiling in on-chip SRAM avoids reading and writing the full score matrix, and the result is exact.

questions.q: Why does MoCo encode its key queue with a slowly updated momentum encoder?
options: Old queued keys stay consistent with current ones, so a big queue works
It averages the loss over a larger effective batch of queries
It replaces BatchNorm, which cannot be applied to the queued keys
It stops gradients flowing back into the images used as queries
questions.why: Queued keys were produced by older encoders. A momentum-updated key encoder changes slowly, so old and new keys remain comparable and the queue can hold thousands of negatives.

questions.q: Which metric is minimised in expectation only when the model reports the true class probabilities?
options: Area under the ROC curve across all thresholds
Brier score (squared error of probabilities)
F1 score maximised over all possible thresholds
Accuracy after thresholding the probabilities at 0.5
questions.why: Brier and log loss are strictly proper scoring rules. Accuracy, F1 and AUC reward only ranking or the side of a threshold, so many different probabilities score equally well.

questions.q: Test-set R² comes out at −0.3. What does it mean?
options: Its predictions are negatively correlated with the true targets
The model predicts worse than a constant prediction at the mean
It explains 30% of the variance, but in the wrong direction
It is a bug, because R² is a squared quantity and cannot be negative
questions.why: R² = 1 − SSE/SST can go below zero when the model's squared error exceeds that of a constant mean predictor. It can happen with overfit or badly shifted models.

questions.q: BatchNorm degrades at 2 images per GPU. What does GroupNorm change to fix this?
options: Statistics come from each sample alone, over groups of channels
It uses running averages from earlier batches, even during training steps
It still normalises across the batch, but over a larger spatial window
It drops the learnable scale and shift so batch noise matters less
questions.why: GroupNorm's mean and variance come from each sample alone (over groups of channels). Nothing depends on how many samples share the batch.

questions.q: Why does rescaling positions (position interpolation) help extend a RoPE model's context?
options: It keeps the rotation angles inside the range seen in training
It gives long inputs extra attention heads to cover the longer range
It lowers attention entropy, so distant tokens get more weight
It shortens the sequence, so attention fits in the available memory
questions.why: RoPE rotates by angle proportional to position. Positions beyond the training length give unseen angles, so interpolating squeezes them back into the trained range.

questions.q: The gap between log p(x) and the ELBO equals which quantity?
options: KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z)), the regulariser term inside the ELBO itself
KL(p(z|x) ‖ q(z|x)), the same divergence in the opposite direction
The reconstruction error E_q[−log p(x|z)] averaged over the data
KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z|x)), the error of the posterior approximation
questions.why: log p(x) = ELBO + KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z|x)). Direction matters: the gap is the KL from q to the true posterior, which is non-negative, hence the bound.

questions.title: Midnight Classification
questions.q: You are training logistic regression to predict whether a shop is busy. It is busy at 23:00, 00:00, and 01:00, but quiet at other hours. Which representation lets logistic regression express this exact pattern with a linear decision boundary?
options: Raw hour as an integer from 0 to 23
Hour standardized to mean 0 and variance 1
sin(2πh/24) and cos(2πh/24)
Squared hour h²
questions.why: On the unit circle, the three busy hours are adjacent and can be separated from all other integer hours by a linear threshold on cosine.

questions.title: The Time Zone Trap
questions.q: You are predicting when people sleep using data from 20 countries. Sleep patterns depend primarily on local hour, but timestamps are stored in UTC. Which preprocessing most directly represents this pattern?
options: Convert timestamps to local time, then make cyclic hour features
Standardize UTC hour
Remove the time zone and retain UTC hour unchanged
Convert timestamps to Unix seconds
questions.why: Local time aligns the human activity pattern across countries; cyclic encoding handles midnight adjacency.

questions.title: The Surprisingly Accurate Medical Model
questions.q: A dataset contains 10 images from each patient. A random image split gives 97% accuracy, but deployment will involve entirely new patients. Which validation split best estimates deployment performance?
options: Stratify individual images by diagnosis
Increase validation fraction from 20% to 40%
Shuffle images more thoroughly
Put all images from each patient into only one split
questions.why: A patient group split prevents identity and correlated imaging conditions leaking between training and validation.

questions.title: Predicting Tomorrow
questions.q: You predict electricity consumption at 14:00 tomorrow from past hourly consumption. Which candidate feature uses unavailable future information?
options: Consumption at 14:00 yesterday
A centered moving average around tomorrow at 14:00
Average consumption over the previous seven days
The hour of day
questions.why: A centered window around the forecast time contains tomorrow's target and later values.

questions.title: The Perfect Identifier
questions.q: A categorical device_id is nearly unique per row. You replace IDs with their average target computed on all training rows, and a classifier gets 100% training accuracy but chance validation accuracy. Which change most directly prevents this encoding from giving each training row its own label?
options: Use labels from other folds to encode each training row
Increase the number of epochs
Standardize encoded values
Add raw device_id as a numerical feature
questions.why: Out of fold target encoding prevents a row's own label from entering its encoded input.

questions.title: Missing Values as Information
questions.q: A lab sensor sometimes returns NaN. Whether a value is missing remains predictive of the label even after accounting for all observed values. What should you add?
options: Impute zero and do nothing else
Discard every incomplete row
Impute and add a binary missingness indicator
Replace every value with its rank
questions.why: A missingness flag preserves the information in the observation process itself.

questions.title: PCA’s Hidden Failure
questions.q: You have independent features x₁ (variance 100, unrelated to the label) and x₂ (variance 0.01, perfectly determines the label). You apply unstandardized PCA and retain one component. In the population limit, what is retained?
options: x₂, because PCA is label aware
x₁, losing the label information
An equal mixture of x₁ and x₂
Whichever has greater mutual information with the label
questions.why: PCA is unsupervised and prioritizes variance, not predictive relevance.

questions.title: A Distance Problem
questions.q: You train KNN with two equally relevant measurements. One numerical column has values around 1; the other has values around 10,000 solely because of its units. You use Euclidean distance. What is the most appropriate first change?
options: Increase k until the unit difference disappears
Apply PCA without scaling
Switch to a regression estimator
Scale features using statistics fitted only on training data
questions.why: Raw Euclidean distance is sensitive to feature units; training only scaling avoids validation leakage.

questions.title: The Miraculous Image Validation
questions.q: You create five crops of every labeled photograph, then randomly split the crops into train and validation. The validation score jumps sharply. What is the cleanest correction?
options: Split the original photographs first, then augment the training originals
Apply more aggressive augmentation to validation crops
Use a larger validation fraction after augmentation
Keep the split and add dropout
questions.why: Crops from one photograph are highly correlated; split at the source image level before augmentation.

questions.title: A Category That Has Never Appeared
questions.q: A model uses one hot encoded country codes. At inference, a previously unseen country appears. Which pipeline is robust without learning preprocessing from validation or test labels?
options: Refit the encoder on the test set alone
Assign the new country the label of the most common training country
Fit the encoder on training data with unknown categories ignored during transform
Replace all country names by their alphabetical positions
questions.why: An encoder fit on training categories with explicit unknown category handling keeps the feature space stable.

questions.title: AUC Without Better Predictions
questions.q: A binary model outputs distinct real valued scores. You replace every score s with sigmoid(5s). In exact arithmetic, what is guaranteed?
options: ROC AUC increases but log loss stays fixed
ROC AUC is unchanged; probability calibration may change
ROC AUC and log loss are both unchanged
ROC AUC decreases because sigmoid compresses large scores
questions.why: A strictly increasing function preserves all score rankings, so it preserves binary ROC AUC but not probability values.

questions.title: The Rare Disease Shift
questions.q: A classifier has unchanged true positive rate and false positive rate in two populations. The disease becomes much rarer, and both rates are strictly between 0 and 1. What happens to precision?
options: It must increase
It stays unchanged because recall stayed unchanged
It equals the false positive rate
It decreases
questions.why: With a lower positive base rate, false positives occupy a larger share of predicted positives.

questions.title: The 95% Accuracy Trap
questions.q: A test set has 95 negative and 5 positive examples. Model A predicts every example negative. Model B gets 4 positives right, misses 1 positive, and wrongly flags 6 negatives. Which has the higher positive class F1?
options: Model A, because its accuracy is higher
Both have F1 = 0.5
Model B, even though its accuracy is lower
Both have equal F1 because the test set is fixed
questions.why: Model A has positive F1 = 0; Model B has F1 = 2·4/(2·4+6+1) = 8/15.

questions.title: The Batch Metric Bug
questions.q: You report test set F1 by computing F1 separately for each minibatch and averaging the batch F1 values. Batches have different class proportions. What computes the true F1 of the complete test set?
options: Take the median batch F1
Concatenate all predictions and targets, then compute F1 once
Weight each batch F1 by the number of examples
Use the mean batch F1 only if batch size is constant
questions.why: F1 is a nonlinear function of total TP, FP, and FN; averaging batch F1 generally gives a different result.

questions.title: The Best of 100 Models
questions.q: You train 100 configurations and pick the one with highest accuracy on one fixed validation set. The winning validation score is unusually high. What is the main statistical concern?
options: The model always has too many parameters
Using a fixed validation set causes training gradients to vanish
Validation accuracy is always an underestimate
Selecting the maximum over noisy validation estimates gives an optimistic winning score
questions.why: Trying many configurations can overfit the validation set even without directly training on its labels.

questions.title: The Overconfident Group
questions.q: Among 1,000 examples receiving predicted probability 0.8, only 500 are actually positive. What can you directly conclude about calibration for this group?
options: The model is overconfident at 0.8
The model has ROC AUC = 0.5
The classifier has recall 50%
The model is underconfident at 0.8
questions.why: For calibrated 0.8 predictions, approximately 80% should be positive; only 50% are.

questions.title: Expensive False Negatives
questions.q: A calibrated model outputs P(y=1|x)=p. A false positive costs 1 unit, a false negative costs 100 units, and correct decisions cost 0. With no other constraints, when should you predict positive?
options: When p > 0.5
When p > 1/101
Only when p = 1
questions.why: Predict positive when expected FP cost 1−p is less than expected FN cost 100p, hence p > 1/101.

questions.title: Lowering the Threshold
questions.q: For a fixed set of binary classifier scores, you lower the threshold used to predict positive. Which statement is guaranteed, assuming the positive class is present?
options: Recall cannot decrease
Precision must decrease
Accuracy must increase
F1 must increase
questions.why: Lowering the threshold never turns a predicted positive into negative, so the number of true positives cannot fall.

questions.title: The Log Transform That Does Nothing
questions.q: You fit an exact greedy decision tree using all candidate threshold partitions. Every value of one positive numerical feature is replaced by its logarithm, which preserves their strict order. What is true about the possible splits on that feature?
options: The best split must move to a different subset
No threshold split is possible after logging
The feature must become less useful
The same training subsets remain achievable by thresholds
questions.why: Strict monotonic transforms preserve ordering; a decision tree threshold still separates the same subsets.

questions.title: XOR with Logistic Regression
questions.q: Two binary inputs x₁ and x₂ have label 1 exactly when one, but not both, is 1. Ordinary logistic regression cannot classify all four possible pairs perfectly. Which extra feature makes linear separation possible?
options: x₁ + x₂
x₁ − x₂
x₁·x₂
A constant bias feature
questions.why: An interaction term permits a decision rule based on x₁+x₂−2x₁x₂, which is 1 only when the inputs differ.

questions.title: Two Rings
questions.q: Unlabeled 2D points form two thin concentric rings separated by a clear empty gap. Which method is naturally suited to recover the two ring shaped clusters?
options: DBSCAN with suitable parameters
Standard KMeans with k=2
One principal component followed by KMeans
A linear separator
questions.why: Density based clustering can identify nonconvex connected regions separated by empty space; centroid methods favor convex groups.

questions.title: One Thousand Copies of the Same Tree
questions.q: You ensemble 1,000 trees. Each tree is identical, trained on the same data, and makes exactly the same predictions. What is the main limitation?
options: Voting reduces errors by a factor of 1,000
Their mistakes are perfectly correlated, so averaging gives no improvement
Ensembling identical models changes the decision boundary dramatically
Identical trees cannot be combined by majority voting
questions.why: If every model outputs the same value, their average and vote equal one tree's output.

questions.title: Units Change the Regularized Model
questions.q: A logistic regression model uses L2 regularization with a fixed penalty coefficient. You convert one input feature from meters to millimeters and retrain without rescaling features. Why might predictions change?
options: Logistic regression cannot accept values above 100
Conversion changes which labels are positive
The L2 penalty acts on coefficients and is not invariant to rescaling one feature
All sigmoid activations become zero on large inputs
questions.why: The coefficient compensates for units, but its squared penalty changes relative to other coefficients.

questions.title: Duplicating a Neighbor
questions.q: For a test point, the three nearest training examples are (distance 0.1, class 1), (0.2, class 0), and (0.3, class 0). A 3NN classifier predicts 0. You add an exact duplicate of the first training example. What does 3NN now predict?
options: Class 1
Class 0
An error because identical points are forbidden
The prediction remains unchanged by definition
questions.why: The three nearest are now two class 1 examples at 0.1 and one class 0 example at 0.2.

questions.title: Which Penalty Can Discard a Feature?
questions.q: You want a linear model to perform feature selection by making some learned coefficients exactly zero. Which penalty is specifically associated with this sparse behavior?
options: An L2 penalty only
An L1 penalty
Neither L1 nor L2 can produce zero coefficients
Increasing batch size
questions.why: L1's nonsmooth penalty at zero encourages exact zeros; L2 typically shrinks coefficients continuously.

questions.title: The Invisible Batch Matrix
questions.q: In PyTorch, predictions have shape (B, 1) and regression labels have shape (B,), with B>1. You pass both directly to nn.MSELoss. What happens?
options: PyTorch always raises a hard shape error
PyTorch silently reshapes labels to (B,1) before the loss
The arrays broadcast to (B,B), producing a wrong pairwise loss (typically with a warning)
The loss uses only the first prediction
questions.why: Broadcasting aligns trailing dimensions, expanding (B,1) and (B,) to (B,B).

questions.title: Four Steps, One Update
questions.q: You accumulate gradients from four equally sized minibatches and take one SGD step. Loss on each minibatch is its mean. Assume no batch dependent layers or other stochastic effects. What is needed to match the full batch mean gradient?
options: Divide each minibatch loss by 4 before backward
Multiply each loss by 4
Call optimizer.step() after every backward
Set every gradient to zero between minibatches
questions.why: Each minibatch mean must contribute one quarter to the average gradient over four equal minibatches.

questions.title: Why Accumulation Is Not Quite a Large Batch
questions.q: You accumulate gradients over four minibatches instead of processing one large batch. Loss scaling is correct, but results still differ when the model uses BatchNorm in training mode. Why?
options: The optimizer is unable to add gradients
The learning rate is automatically divided by four
BatchNorm disables backpropagation during accumulation
BatchNorm computes normalization statistics separately on each small minibatch
questions.why: Gradient accumulation cannot reproduce large batch BatchNorm statistics merely by rescaling losses.

questions.title: A Head That Never Trains
questions.q: You create an optimizer, then replace model.fc with a new nn.Linear layer. The new parameters have requires_grad=True and receive gradients, but they never update. What is the most likely reason?
options: The backbone is in eval mode
The optimizer does not contain the newly created layer's parameters
A new nn.Linear cannot be trained by SGD
requires_grad=True prevents optimizer updates
questions.why: Optimizers retain parameter references from construction time and do not automatically discover replacement layers.

questions.title: Frozen But Still Changing
questions.q: You set requires_grad=False on every parameter of a pretrained BatchNorm backbone, but leave model.train() active while training a new head. Which backbone state can still change?
options: The frozen convolution weights
The frozen BatchNorm affine gamma parameters
BatchNorm running mean and running variance
All requires_grad=False parameters
questions.why: BatchNorm running statistics are buffers that update in training mode even when its parameters are frozen.

questions.title: Two Inference Switches
questions.q: You want standard Dropout disabled, BatchNorm to use stored statistics, and PyTorch not to construct an autograd graph for inference. Which combination achieves all three?
options: model.eval() and torch.no_grad()
model.eval() alone
torch.no_grad() alone
optimizer.zero_grad() and model.train()
questions.why: eval controls module behavior, while no_grad separately disables gradient recording.

questions.title: A Confident Numerical Disaster
questions.q: A binary classifier produces an extremely negative logit for a positive label. You want to compute stable binary cross entropy directly from logits. Which PyTorch option is designed for this?
options: torch.nn.MSELoss on logits
sigmoid followed by torch.log manually
torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss applied to a single logit
torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss on the raw logits
questions.why: BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and the loss in a numerically stable computation.

questions.title: Two Independent Lookups
questions.q: One attention layer must retrieve a color description from one token and a position description from a different token, with independently chosen attention weights. Which design most directly provides two separate attention distributions?
options: Increase only the value dimension of a single head
Use two attention heads with separately learned queries and keys
Remove the softmax from one head
Apply the same attention weights twice
questions.why: Each head can learn its own query/key attention matrix, unlike a single softmax shared across all value channels.

questions.title: Patch Order Without Position
questions.q: A Transformer image classifier has a fixed CLS token, tokenwise operations, full self attention, and no positional information. At inference, you permute all patch tokens but leave CLS in place. What happens to the final CLS embedding?
options: It stays identical in exact arithmetic
It becomes a corresponding permutation of itself
It necessarily changes because attention is order sensitive
All attention probabilities become uniform
questions.why: Without positional information, permuting patch inputs only permutes patch outputs; the fixed CLS output is invariant.

questions.title: A Smaller Patch, a Larger Bill
questions.q: A vision Transformer processes 224×224 images with nonoverlapping 16×16 patches. You change the patch size to 8×8. Ignoring CLS and other special tokens, how does the number of patch to patch attention scores change?
questions.why: Patch count grows from 14²=196 to 28²=784 (4×); pairwise attention scores grow by 4²=16×.

questions.title: The Cheating Language Model
questions.q: An autoregressive language model gets nearly perfect training next token accuracy but fails at generating text. You discover that during training each position could attend to later positions containing target tokens. What should have prevented this?
options: Layer normalization
A larger vocabulary
Dropout on the output head
A causal attention mask
questions.why: Causal masking blocks access to future tokens, preserving the intended next token prediction task.

questions.title: Segmentation Masks That Invent Classes
questions.q: You resize a semantic segmentation image and its integer class mask. After resizing, the mask contains values between class IDs that never existed originally. What is the likely error?
options: You used nearest neighbor interpolation for the mask
You used bilinear interpolation for the class mask instead of nearest neighbor
You normalized RGB channels
You set the image size to a multiple of 32
questions.why: Bilinear interpolation blends class IDs; nearest neighbor interpolation preserves discrete labels.

questions.title: The Flipped Bounding Box
questions.q: An image uses continuous horizontal coordinates from 0 to W=100. A bounding box spans x₁=10 to x₂=30. You flip the image horizontally. What should its new horizontal bounds be?
questions.why: Under a horizontal flip x becomes W−x, so (x₁,x₂) maps to (W−x₂,W−x₁).

questions.title: A Nearly Perfect Segmenter
questions.q: Exactly 98% of pixels in a test image are background and 2% are foreground objects. A model predicts every pixel as background. Which statement is correct?
options: Pixel accuracy is 98%, but foreground IoU is 0
Pixel accuracy is 100% because background dominates
Foreground IoU is 98%
Foreground recall is 98%
questions.why: All background pixels are correct, but no foreground pixel is correctly predicted.

questions.title: An Augmentation That Lies
questions.q: You classify cropped handwritten digits, including 6 and 9. Some rotations turn a valid 6 into an apparent 9, but the augmentation preserves the original label. What is the risk?
options: Rotation never affects digit identity
It only changes the normalization statistics
It guarantees invariance and higher accuracy
It creates contradictory labels, potentially hurting learning
questions.why: Not every image transformation preserves the semantic label; label violating augmentation introduces supervision noise.

questions.title: Same Words, Different Meaning
questions.q: A classifier using only unordered word counts receives "the cat chased the dog" and "the dog chased the cat". The intended labels differ according to who chased whom. What is its fundamental limitation?
options: It cannot count the total number of words
Unigram counts discard word order, so both inputs have the same representation
It lacks enough training epochs
It cannot process repeated words
questions.why: Bag of words is invariant to token permutations; ngrams or an order aware encoder can preserve the distinction.

questions.title: Short Texts Look Small
questions.q: A text encoder pads every sequence to 128 tokens with zero padding vectors, then simply averages all 128 embeddings. Short documents produce much smaller average vector magnitudes than long ones. What is the most direct correction?
options: Add more padding tokens
Train a larger tokenizer vocabulary
Average only over real tokens using a padding mask
Sort all tokens alphabetically before pooling
questions.why: Masked pooling divides the sum by the actual number of real tokens, not the padded length.

questions.title: The Resampling Shortcut
questions.q: An audio clip contains 16,000 PCM samples captured at 16,000 samples per second. A model expects 8,000 samples per second. You change only the sample rate metadata to 8,000, leaving the sample array unchanged. What happens on playback?
options: Duration stays 1 second and pitch stays the same
Duration stays 1 second but pitch doubles
Duration halves to 0.5 seconds
Duration becomes 2 seconds and pitch is halved
questions.why: 16,000 samples at 8,000 samples/second play for two seconds; correct resampling changes the sample data.

questions.title: The Crop That Removes the Label
questions.q: In a binary vision task, y=1 means the target object is visible somewhere in the image. You crop a positive image so the object is completely excluded, but keep y=1. What is wrong?
options: The crop is now mislabeled for the stated task
Cropping positive images can never be used
The crop becomes a valid positive because the original image was positive
Only the learning rate must change
questions.why: An augmentation that removes the target object violates the labeling rule unless the label is updated.

questions.title: The Speaker and the Room
questions.q: You recognize known speakers from short audio clips. Every recording session contains many clips, and room acoustics stay constant within a session. Deployment will use new sessions in new rooms. Which validation design is most revealing, assuming each speaker has recordings in multiple rooms?
options: Randomly split individual frames from every clip
Hold out whole sessions and rooms while keeping the speakers represented in training
Randomly split clips from the same sessions
Duplicate rare speakers' clips before making a random split
questions.why: Whole session and room holdouts test speaker identity rather than memorizing recording conditions.

questions.title: Can You Tell Train from Test?
questions.q: You label training rows 0 and test rows 1, use features only, and train a classifier to tell them apart. Its cross-validated ROC AUC is 0.97. What does this most directly indicate?
options: Train and test differ in distribution, so random validation may mislead
The features are strongly predictive of the original task labels
Test labels have leaked into the training data through shared features
The classifier has overfit, so its cross-validated AUC carries no meaning
questions.why: A classifier that separates train from test exposes covariate shift, so a validation set drawn randomly from train will not mimic test conditions.

questions.title: Filling Holes with the Mean
questions.q: A feature has variance 4. At random, 30% of its values go missing, independently of everything else. You replace each missing value with the mean of the observed ones. Roughly what is the feature's variance afterwards?
options: About 4.0
About 2.8
About 2.0
About 1.2
questions.why: Imputed entries add no squared deviation but still count in n, so the variance shrinks to about 0.7 × 4 = 2.8.

questions.title: Balanced Training, Rare Reality
questions.q: To train faster you discard negatives until 50% of the training rows are positive, while only 1% of real cases are. The model, calibrated on the balanced data, outputs 0.80 for a new case. Assuming only class proportions differ, what is its true probability of being positive?
options: About 0.01
About 0.04
About 0.40
About 0.80
questions.why: Undersampling inflates the odds, so multiply by the real prior odds 0.01/0.99 (balanced prior odds are 1): 4 × 0.0101 ≈ 0.04 odds, hence p ≈ 0.04.

questions.title: The Hidden Ceiling
questions.q: In a binary test set, 10% of the labels are flipped at random, independently of the inputs. A model has 90% accuracy against the clean labels. What accuracy does it measure against the noisy labels?
questions.why: It agrees with a noisy label when it is right and the label intact (0.9 × 0.9) or wrong and the label flipped (0.1 × 0.1): 0.82.

questions.title: A Chance Baseline
questions.q: Only 2% of examples are positive. A model assigns scores that are random and unrelated to the label. What are its expected ROC AUC and average precision (area under the precision-recall curve)?
options: ROC AUC 0.5 and average precision 0.5
ROC AUC 0.02 and average precision 0.02
ROC AUC 0.98 and average precision 0.02
ROC AUC 0.5 and average precision 0.02
questions.why: Random scores give AUC 0.5, but precision at every recall level equals the 2% positive rate, so average precision is about 0.02.

questions.title: Accurate but Overconfident
questions.q: A balanced binary classifier has 85% validation accuracy and a validation log loss of 0.80 nats. A model that always outputs probability 0.5 scores ln 2 ≈ 0.69. What does the comparison show?
options: Its probabilities are worse than constant ones, from confident errors
It must beat the constant model, since accuracy is far above 50%
The log loss must be a bug, since it cannot exceed ln 2
Log loss and accuracy always rank models in exactly the same order
questions.why: Log loss punishes confident mistakes without bound, so an accurate model can still assign worse probabilities than a model that always says 0.5.

questions.title: The Step That Is Too Long
questions.q: You minimise f(w) = 5w² (second derivative 10) with plain gradient descent from w = 1. Which fixed learning rate makes the iterates diverge?
questions.why: Each step multiplies w by 1 − 10·lr, which exceeds magnitude 1 only when lr > 0.2: 0.25 gives −1.5, while 0.15 gives −0.5 and still converges.

questions.title: Points That Do Not Matter
questions.q: You fit a linear soft-margin SVM, then delete one training point that is correctly classified and lies well outside the margin, and refit. What happens to the hyperplane?
options: It shifts slightly toward the class of the deleted point
It shifts slightly away from the class of the deleted point
It keeps its direction but the margin must widen
It is exactly the same hyperplane as before
questions.why: Only support vectors, the points on or inside the margin, have nonzero dual weights, so removing any other point leaves the solution unchanged.

questions.title: Fitting Forever
questions.q: Logistic regression with no regularisation is trained by gradient descent on linearly separable data, for an unlimited number of steps. What happens to the weight vector?
options: Its norm grows without bound as the loss keeps falling
It converges to a finite maximum-likelihood solution
It oscillates around the separating boundary indefinitely
Its norm shrinks toward zero once every point is fit
questions.why: On separable data, scaling the weights up always lowers the loss, so no finite minimiser exists and the norm keeps growing.

questions.title: Counting Evidence Twice
questions.q: A Gaussian Naive Bayes classifier uses a feature x. You append an exact copy of x as a second feature and retrain. How does the log-likelihood ratio that x contributes to the prediction change?
options: It is split evenly between the copies, leaving predictions unchanged
It doubles, making the predicted probabilities overconfident
It is unchanged, since Naive Bayes ignores correlated features
It cancels, since the copy carries no new information
questions.why: Naive Bayes multiplies per-feature likelihoods as if they were independent, so the copy's identical likelihood ratio is counted a second time.

questions.title: Decay That Depends on Gradients
questions.q: In PyTorch, Adam(weight_decay=λ) adds λw to each gradient before Adam divides by the running RMS of gradients, whereas AdamW shrinks weights directly. How does Adam's shrinkage differ between weights?
options: Weights with large typical gradients are shrunk less than those with small ones
Weights with large typical gradients are shrunk more than those with small ones
All weights shrink at the same relative rate, exactly as in AdamW
Only weights whose loss gradient is exactly zero are shrunk
questions.why: The L2 term is divided by the gradient RMS like any gradient, so large-gradient weights get weaker effective decay; AdamW's decay bypasses that division.

questions.title: A Louder Loss
questions.q: To 'strengthen the signal', a colleague multiplies the loss by 1000 and keeps the learning rate. Ignoring ε and weight decay, how do the parameter updates change for plain SGD and for Adam?
options: Both optimisers take steps that are 1000× larger
SGD steps stay the same; Adam steps become 1000× larger
Neither changes, since the learning rate is fixed
SGD steps become 1000× larger; Adam steps stay the same
questions.why: SGD's step is lr × gradient, so it scales with the loss; Adam divides the gradient by its running RMS, which scales identically and cancels.

questions.title: A Softer Target
questions.q: Cross-entropy uses label smoothing 0.1 on 10 classes, so the true class has target 0.91 and every other class 0.01. At the loss minimum, how much larger is the true-class logit than each other logit?
options: About 2.2
About 4.5
About 91
It grows without bound, as with hard labels
questions.why: The softmax must equal the targets, so e^gap = 0.91/0.01 = 91 and the gap is ln 91 ≈ 4.5, which is finite.

questions.title: The Scheduler That Hates Progress
questions.q: You call scheduler.step(val_acc) on ReduceLROnPlateau(optimizer, mode='min', patience=3). Validation accuracy improves every epoch. What happens to the learning rate?
options: It stays constant, because the metric keeps improving every epoch
PyTorch raises an error, because accuracy is not a loss function
It is cut after a few epochs, even though accuracy keeps improving
It rises each epoch, because the metric is steadily increasing
questions.why: In min mode a higher metric counts as no improvement, so once the patience runs out the scheduler cuts the learning rate; accuracy needs mode='max'.

questions.title: Scale-Free Weights
questions.q: A bias-free conv layer feeds a BatchNorm layer in training mode (ε negligible). You multiply the conv weights by 10, and the loss is unchanged. How does the gradient of the loss with respect to those conv weights change?
options: It is divided by 10
It is unchanged
It is multiplied by 10
It is divided by 100
questions.why: BatchNorm makes the loss depend only on w divided by its norm, so L(cw) = L(w), and differentiating gives ∇L(cw) = ∇L(w)/c.

questions.title: A Fading Signal
questions.q: A 10-layer MLP of width 512 stacks Linear + ReLU blocks without biases. Weights are drawn from N(0, 1/512) and the inputs have mean-square 1. Roughly what is the mean-square of the activations after the tenth ReLU?
options: About 0.001
About 0.5
About 1
About 1000
questions.why: A ReLU keeps half the energy, so each layer halves the mean-square, leaving 0.5¹⁰ ≈ 0.001; He initialisation uses variance 2/fan_in to compensate.

questions.title: A Spike in a Quiet Run
questions.q: Adam (β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999) has seen gradients of about 0.001 for 2,000 steps. One step then delivers a gradient of 1. Roughly how large is that update, in units of the learning rate?
options: About 1000
About 3
About 1
About 0.001
questions.why: Momentum rises by 0.1·g but the variance estimate by only 0.001·g², so the step is about 0.1/√0.001 ≈ 3 times the learning rate.

questions.title: Variance of a Dot Product
questions.q: Query and key entries are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, and d_k = 64. Which constant c makes q·k / c have variance 1?
