questions.why: q·k sums 64 independent unit-variance products, so its variance is 64 and its standard deviation 8; dividing by √d_k restores variance 1.

questions.title: The Cache Bill
questions.q: A decoder has 32 layers and head size 128. It uses grouped-query attention: 32 query heads share 8 key/value heads. Keys and values are cached in fp16. How much cache memory does each generated token add?
options: 512 KiB
256 KiB
128 KiB
64 KiB
questions.why: Per token: 2 (keys and values) × 32 layers × 8 heads × 128 dims × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB, a quarter of full multi-head attention.

questions.title: Rotations Remember Offsets
questions.q: Rotary embeddings rotate each 2D pair of the query at position m by angle mθ, and of the key at position n by angle nθ. For fixed q and k, how does that pair's contribution to q·k depend on m and n?
options: Only through the offset m − n, not the absolute positions
Only through the sum m + n, not the individual positions
Through m and n separately, never through their difference
Not at all, since rotations preserve the length of vectors
questions.why: Rotating both vectors by a common angle leaves their dot product unchanged, so rotations by mθ and nθ are equivalent to a single rotation by (m − n)θ.

questions.title: A Bias That Cancels
questions.q: In one attention head you add the same learned vector b to every key before computing scores. What happens to the attention weights?
options: They flatten toward uniform, since every key shifts equally
They shift toward keys at later positions in the sequence
They sharpen on the keys with the largest norm
They are unchanged, because q·b is identical for every key
questions.why: Each score becomes q·k_j + q·b, and softmax is unchanged when the same constant is added to every score in a row.

questions.title: How Far Does a Window Reach?
questions.q: In a causal Transformer, each token attends only to itself and the 3 tokens before it. After 5 such layers, the output at position p can depend on tokens as far back as position p − what?
questions.why: Each layer lets information hop back 3 positions, and hops compose across layers, so 5 layers reach 5 × 3 = 15 positions back.

questions.title: Where the Compute Goes
questions.q: A Transformer layer has d_model = 768, a feed-forward hidden size of 4d, and sequence length 1,024. Per token, which costs more multiply-adds: the projection and feed-forward matrices, or the query-key scores plus the weighted sum of values?
options: Scores and weighting, by roughly 4.5×
Scores and weighting, because attention is quadratic in length
They cost about the same at this length
Projections and feed-forward, by roughly 4.5×
questions.why: Projections and feed-forward cost 12d² ≈ 7.1M multiply-adds per token versus 2nd ≈ 1.6M for scores and weighting; attention only dominates beyond n ≈ 6d ≈ 4,600.

questions.title: A Pool in the Middle
questions.q: A CNN applies a 3×3 conv (stride 1), another 3×3 conv (stride 1), a 2×2 max-pool (stride 2), then a 3×3 conv (stride 1). How wide, in input pixels, is the receptive field of one final output unit?
options: 7 pixels
9 pixels
10 pixels
12 pixels
questions.why: The two convs reach 5, the pool adds 1 more (6) and doubles the step between units, so the last 3×3 conv adds 2 × 2 = 4, giving 10.

questions.title: Upsampling Off by One
questions.q: nn.ConvTranspose2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1) with no output_padding upsamples a 16×16 feature map. What is the output side length?
questions.why: Output = (in − 1)·stride − 2·padding + kernel = 15·2 − 2 + 3 = 31; output_padding=1 would be needed to reach 32.

questions.title: Half a Step
questions.q: A stride-2 convolution with circular padding processes a 1D signal. You feed it the signal shifted by 2 samples, then shifted by 1 sample. Which statement holds?
options: Shift by 2 gives a shifted output; shift by 1 generally does not
Both shifts give shifted outputs, since convolution is shift-equivariant
A shift by 1 gives the output shifted by half a sample
Neither shift gives a shifted output, because stride destroys equivariance
questions.why: Stride 2 samples every second position, so only even shifts map onto shifted outputs; an odd shift samples different positions, which is aliasing.

questions.title: Two Overlap Scores
questions.q: A predicted foreground mask has IoU 0.5 with the ground truth. What is its Dice coefficient, which equals the F1 score on the foreground pixels?
questions.why: IoU = TP/(TP+FP+FN) and Dice = 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN), so Dice = 2·IoU/(1+IoU) = 1/1.5 ≈ 0.67.

questions.title: One Channel to Three
questions.q: A pretrained CNN's first conv takes 3 input channels. To accept grayscale images you swap in a 1-channel conv with the same bias. Which weights reproduce exactly what the network computed on grayscale images copied into all 3 channels?
options: The mean of the three channels' filters
The first channel's filters alone
The sum of the three channels' filters
The first channel's filters multiplied by 3
questions.why: With one image g in all channels, the output is (w₁ + w₂ + w₃) convolved with g, so the sum is exact; the mean gives a third.

questions.title: A Thousand Whispers
questions.q: A dense detector scores 100,000 anchors per image, of which 100 are positives. With cross-entropy, each easy negative has loss 0.01 and each positive has loss 2. Which part contributes more to the summed loss?
options: The positives, since each one's loss is 200 times larger
Neither: positives and negatives each contribute about half
The easy negatives contribute almost nothing, as each loss is tiny
The easy negatives, outweighing the positives about five to one
questions.why: 99,900 easy negatives × 0.01 ≈ 1,000 against 100 positives × 2 = 200, so the swarm of easy examples swamps the rare hard ones; focal loss addresses this.

questions.title: Perplexity Across Tokenizers
questions.q: On the same text, model A predicts whole words and has perplexity 100 per word. Model B predicts subword tokens, 2.5 per word on average, and has perplexity 8 per token. Which model needs fewer bits to encode the text?
options: Model A, at about 6.6 bits per word against 7.5
Model B, because its perplexity of 8 is far lower than 100
Model B, at about 3 bits per word against 6.6
They tie, since both perplexities are measured on the same text
questions.why: Perplexity is per prediction unit, so convert to bits per word: log₂100 ≈ 6.6 for A versus 2.5 × log₂8 = 7.5 for B.

questions.title: The Double L
questions.q: A CTC speech model must output the word 'hello' (h, e, l, l, o) from T encoder frames. What is the smallest T for which at least one valid alignment exists?
questions.why: Adjacent repeated letters collapse unless a blank separates them, so 'hello' needs its 5 letters plus one blank between the two l's: 6 frames.

questions.title: A Tone From Nowhere
questions.q: A recorder samples at 16 kHz with no anti-aliasing filter, while a pure 10 kHz tone is in the air. Where does the tone appear in the spectrum of the recording?
options: At 10 kHz, since sampling does not change frequencies
Nowhere, because frequencies above 8 kHz are discarded
At 8 kHz, clipped to the highest representable frequency
At 6 kHz, folded back about the Nyquist frequency
questions.why: Sampling at 16 kHz folds a frequency f above 8 kHz down to |f − 16 kHz|, so 10 kHz aliases to 6 kHz.

questions.title: How Far Back Does It Listen?
questions.q: A causal 1D conv stack has kernel size 2 and dilations 1, 2, 4, …, 512 (ten layers, stride 1). Audio is sampled at 16 kHz. About how much audio does a single output sample depend on?
options: About 128 ms
About 64 ms
About 32 ms
About 0.6 ms
questions.why: Each layer adds (k − 1)·dilation samples: 1 + 2 + … + 512 = 1023, plus the sample itself gives 1024 samples, which is 64 ms at 16 kHz.

questions.title: Nucleus Arithmetic
questions.q: Next-token probabilities are 0.50, 0.30, 0.10, 0.06 and 0.04. You sample with top-p = 0.85: keep the smallest set of top tokens whose total probability is at least 0.85, renormalise, then sample. What is the probability of picking the top token?
questions.why: The smallest set reaching 0.85 is the top three tokens, with total mass 0.90, so the top token has 0.50/0.90 ≈ 0.56.

questions.title: Shape of a Spectrogram
questions.q: torch.stft is applied to 1 second of 16 kHz audio (16,000 samples) with n_fft = 400, hop_length = 160, center=True and one-sided complex output. What is the output shape (frequency bins, frames)?
questions.why: A one-sided FFT of 400 points has 400/2 + 1 = 201 bins, and center padding gives 1 + 16000/160 = 101 frames.
